definition: Avant-garde means radically new and experimental, especially in art.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word avant-garde. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know avant-garde should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The choreographer's avant-garde piece unfolded in a parking garage, with dancers partnered by slow-moving forklifts.
Fresh praises a small newness — a fresh take on a sandwich — and stops far short of avant-garde.
Experimental goes further than fresh — the thing is being run as a test, kept or dropped by its results — but it stops short of avant-garde, which breaks with every model that came before.

Cutting-edge means at the newest stage of development, and it is said mostly of technology — chips, labs, techniques at the frontier. Avant-garde belongs to art and carries defiance: radically new work out ahead of its entire field. A phone can be cutting-edge while perfectly conventional in spirit; avant-garde work breaks with the models themselves.

Groundbreaking praises a genuine first — the study, device, or ruling that opens territory no one had entered — and it works in any field. Avant-garde adds a posture: radical newness out ahead of a whole artistic field, past where any earlier model can guide it. A vaccine can be groundbreaking; a ballet staged in a freight elevator is avant-garde.

Avant-garde is more precise than 'new' or even 'experimental' because it means radically new and experimental, especially in art — the word is French for the advance guard, the soldiers sent ahead of the army.
An avant-garde work is out in front of its whole field, past the point where any earlier model can guide it.
Avant-garde belongs to the arts and to writing about them: it says a work is radically new, out ahead of its whole field.
For a new method in a lab or a classroom, experimental is the honest word; for something merely up to date, cutting-edge.
In this unit, compare nascent, which says a thing has only just come into existence, whether or not it is daring.

When the Meridian Ensemble premiered 'Weather Systems,' the ushers handed out no programs, because the piece had no movements to list.
The audience sat scattered among the players, and the score asked each musician to improvise from barometer readings taken that afternoon.
Critics called the work avant-garde, and the label fit: it discarded melody, fixed seating, and the concert ritual itself in a single evening.
One reviewer walked out before the end; another wrote that the ensemble had pushed past every model the concert hall had ever supplied.
The players themselves shrugged off both verdicts, saying only that the old forms had stopped asking questions worth answering.
